title: Horizontal, Vertical and Hybrid Microinstruction Formats
quickIdea: Horizontal microcode gives every control signal its own bit: wide words, no decoder, any number of signals at once. Vertical microcode encodes a group of signals into a binary field: narrow words, one decoder, at most one signal from that group at a time. Hybrid encodes only the groups whose members can never fire together.
remember: Horizontal: one bit per control signal, so width equals the number of signals and no decoder is needed in the path.
Vertical: a group of n mutually exclusive signals needs ceil(log2(n + 1)) bits, the +1 being the no-operation code.
The trade is exact: vertical saves bits and costs a decoder delay, and it also makes it impossible to assert two members of one group together.
Hybrid, also called diagonal, groups only the signals that are genuinely mutually exclusive - the bus-source field, the ALU-function field - and leaves the rest as single bits.
The rule to memorise: a group may be encoded only if its members can never be needed simultaneously. If two signals must fire together, they must be in different fields or both horizontal.

example.prompt: A unit has 25 control signals and at most two may be active at any one time. How many bits does a horizontal word need, and what is the smallest vertical encoding?
example.work: Horizontal: 25 bits. Vertical: two fields, each choosing one of 25 signals, so each needs ceil(log2 25) = 5 bits, and the word is 10 bits. If the two fields were merged into one field choosing an unordered pair, the number of states would be 1 + 25 + 300 = 326, which needs 9 bits - but then the two signals would have no order, and a decoder for 326 states is far larger than two 5-bit decoders.
example.answer: 25 bits horizontally against 10 bits vertically. The 9-bit figure is the information-theoretic floor, not the accepted exam answer.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 1996 Q.2.25 is this example and its accepted answer is 10 bits, read as two 5-bit fields. GATE CSE 1997 Q.5.3 is the same arithmetic split across two kinds of signal - 2 bits for none-or-one-of-three and 6 bits for any subset of six, giving 8. GATE CSE 2002 Q.2.7 tests the properties of the horizontal form, where all three statements - no decoders, larger than vertical, one bit per signal - are true.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 1997 Q.5.3: a microinstruction is to specify none or one of three micro-operations of one kind, and none or up to six micro-operations of another kind. The minimum number of bits in the microinstruction is (A) 9 (B) 5 (C) 8 (D) none of the above.
variations.why: The first kind is mutually exclusive, so 4 states (none, or one of three) take 2 bits. The second kind allows any subset of six, so 2^6 = 64 states take 6 bits. 2 + 6 = 8. Answering 9 means encoding the first kind horizontally, which is not the minimum.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A control word has three fields of mutually exclusive signals holding 4, 6 and 9 signals, plus 7 signals that may be asserted freely. Give the vertical width and the horizontal width.
variations.why: Each encoded field costs ceil(log2(n + 1)): ceil(log2 5) = 3, ceil(log2 7) = 3, ceil(log2 10) = 4. The seven free signals cannot be encoded at all and stay one bit each.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does vertical microcode cost speed even though it saves memory?
variations.answer: Because every encoded field must pass through a decoder before it becomes a control signal, so the decoder's delay sits in the path from the control store to the datapath.
variations.why: That single extra delay is the whole reason the speed order is hardwired, then horizontal, then vertical, which is what GATE CSE 1999 Q.2.19 asks for.

trap.what: Encoding two signals into one vertical field when they can be needed at the same time.
trap.why: A field holds one code, so it can select one of its members; two signals that must both be active have no code that expresses both.
trap.counterexample: Putting memory-read and PC-increment in one 1-bit field looks like a saving, but the fetch step asserts both at once, so the machine can no longer fetch. They belong in two separate bits.

check.question: How many bits does a vertical field need for a group of 12 mutually exclusive signals, and why is it not 4 bits of plain binary?
check.answer: 4 bits, because 12 + 1 = 13 states and 2^4 = 16 covers them. What the 4 bits are not is 12 signals in 12 bits: that is the horizontal form.
check.explanation: The +1 is the no-operation code, and it is what makes a 3-signal group need 2 bits (4 states) rather than 2 bits for 3 states only. 16 codes cover 13, so four bits suffice with three codes left over.
